  time series can contain.

::: {.charcoal}
Donnelly puts forecasting in Chapter 16, the last chapter of the book. We are
reading part of it in Week 3, and we will come back to it twice more. Two
reasons. First, forecasting is the most immediately *useful* thing in the
book, and it is the one you will be asked to do at work before anyone asks
you for a hypothesis test. Second, it is a skill, not a fact — it needs
practice, and one week in December is not practice. So for the rest of the

challenge**, and this note is the equipment you need to start.

# What Forecasting Is

::: {.blue}
**Qualitative forecasting** relies primarily on a knowledgeable person's
intuition and judgment to predict events. **Quantitative forecasting** uses
historical data and mathematics.
:::

Every business decision that takes time to carry out — hiring, ordering
inventory, building a plant, scheduling staff for a convention weekend — is a
bet on a number nobody knows yet. A forecast is the number you bet on, and a
forecasting *method* is a rule for producing it that you could apply again next
period. The second half of that sentence is what separates a method from a
guess.

::: {.blue}
A **time series** is a group of data values, each associated with a specific
point in time.
:::

Donnelly's running example is Brandywine Ford, a dealership that wants to
forecast next quarter's new-car sales from the last twelve quarters (Table
16.1). We will use it throughout, because you can check every number against
the book. Then we will do the same thing to the CPI.

```{python}
#| label: car-sales-table
CAR_SALES.to_frame("sales").T
```

The first thing a forecaster does is *plot the series*. A table hides what a
picture shows.

```{python}
#| label: car-sales-plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
x = np.arange(1, 13)
ax.plot(x, CAR_SALES.values, color=UNLV_SCARLET, marker="o", linewidth=1.4)
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xlabel("Period (quarters, 2016Q1 = 1)")
ax.set_ylabel("New cars sold")
ax.set_title("Brandywine Ford new car sales (Donnelly Table 16.1)", color=UNLV_SCARLET)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6")
for side in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

## The Components of a Time Series

::: {.blue}
A **trend component** is present if a general upward or downward movement can
be seen in the data.

A **seasonal component** is present if a consistent pattern can be associated
with the calendar. Seasonal patterns repeat within a year, so you need data
more often than annual to see them.

A **cyclical component** is movement that results from swings in the economy
over several years — longer than a season.

The **random component** is whatever is left: movement that cannot be
attributed to trend, season, or cycle. It is often called *noise*.
:::

Look back at the car sales. The line drifts upward (trend), and every second
and fourth quarter spikes (seasonal). Now look at the five challenge series.
The CPI is almost pure trend. Initial claims are almost pure noise around a
level. Visitor volume has a calendar in it — you can see March and October. The
Nevada house price index trends, but not in a straight line, and it has the
2008 cycle in its long history.

::: {.charcoal}
Every method in Chapter 16 is a bet about which components are present. The
methods in *this* note assume there is a level and some noise, and nothing
else. When that is wrong — when there is a trend or a season — they fail in a
predictable direction, and you will see it happen to the CPI below. Knowing
*how* a method fails is most of knowing when to use it.
:::

# Smoothing Methods

::: {.blue}
The goal of a **smoothing method** is to average out the random movements in
a time series, because they are unpredictable. If the forecast is an average
of recent values, the ups and downs of the random component should cancel.
:::

Smoothing works best when the series is fairly consistent over time: no
significant trend, seasonal, or cyclical component. Chapter 16 covers four
smoothing methods. We take the first two now and add a fifth that the book
skips, because it is the one every other method has to beat.

## The Naive Forecast

::: {.blue}
The **naive forecast** for period $t$ is the actual value from period $t-1$:

$$F_t = A_{t-1}.$$
:::

"Next quarter will be like this quarter." It sounds like an insult to
forecasting, and for many series it is remarkably hard to beat — the CPI, as
you are about to see, is one of them. A method that cannot outperform the naive
forecast has not earned its complexity. Always compute it first.

```{python}
#| label: naive-cars
nv = naive_forecast(CAR_SALES)
error_table(CAR_SALES, nv).round(1)[["actual", "forecast", "error", "abs_error"]]
```

The naive forecast for 2019Q1 is `{python} num(nv.iloc[-1], 0)` cars — the
2018Q4 figure. Notice the pattern in the error column: it alternates sign,
because the series alternates high and low quarters and the naive forecast is
always one step behind. That is the seasonal component punishing a method that
does not know about seasons.

## The Simple Moving Average

::: {.blue}
A **simple moving average** (SMA) forecast averages the most recent $p$ values
of the series:

$$\text{SMA}(p, t) = \frac{A_{t-1} + A_{t-2} + \cdots + A_{t-p}}{p}.$$
:::

Donnelly chooses $p = 3$ and forecasts the first quarter of 2019 from the last
three quarters of 2018:

```{python}
#| label: sma3-math
#| output: asis
a = CAR_SALES.values
show_math(r"\text{SMA}(p=3,\ 2019\text{Q1}) = \frac{%d + %d + %d}{3} = \frac{%d}{3} = %.1f \approx %d"
          % (a[-3], a[-2], a[-1], a[-3:].sum(), a[-3:].mean(), round(a[-3:].mean())))
```

Now the question your boss asks: *how good is that number likely to be?* The
only honest way to answer is to pretend you had used the method all along, and
measure how it did. Apply the three-period average to the history: the first
forecast it can make is for period 4 (it needs periods 1–3), and so on.

```{python}
#| label: sma3-table
sma3 = sma_forecast(CAR_SALES, 3)
error_table(CAR_SALES, sma3).round(1)[["actual", "forecast", "error", "abs_error"]]
```

::: {.scarlet}
**The mistake students make most:** assigning the average of periods 1–3 to
period 3. A forecast is for a period you do not yet know. The average of
periods 1, 2 and 3 is the forecast *for period 4*. If you slide it back one row
the method looks far better than it is, because it is being credited with
knowing the value it was supposed to predict.
:::

## Measuring Accuracy: the Mean Absolute Deviation

::: {.blue}
The **mean absolute deviation** (MAD) is the average size of the forecasting
error over the periods that have a forecast (Formula 16.1):

$$\text{MAD} = \frac{\sum |A_t - F_t|}{n},$$

where $A_t$ is the actual value in period $t$, $F_t$ the forecast for period
$t$, and $n$ the number of forecasting errors.
:::

The absolute value matters. If the forecast is 10 too high one quarter and 10
too low the next, the average *error* is zero — which would be a lie about a
method that missed by 10 every time. The average *absolute* error is 10.

```{python}
#| label: sma3-mad
#| output: asis
t3 = error_table(CAR_SALES, sma3).dropna()
show_math(r"\text{MAD}_{\text{SMA}(3)} = \frac{%s}{%d} = \frac{%.1f}{%d} = %.1f"
          % (" + ".join(f"{v:.1f}" for v in t3["abs_error"]), len(t3),
             t3["abs_error"].sum(), len(t3), t3["abs_error"].mean()))
```

A three-period moving average would have missed by about `{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, sma3))`
cars a quarter. Whether that is acceptable is a business question, not a
statistical one. Whether it is *better than the alternatives* is a statistical
one, and it is answered by computing the alternatives.

### What if $p = 4$?

```{python}
#| label: sma4
sma4 = sma_forecast(CAR_SALES, 4)
error_table(CAR_SALES, sma4).round(1)[["actual", "forecast", "error", "abs_error"]]
```

The four-period forecast for 2019Q1 is `{python} num(sma4.iloc[-1])` with a MAD of
`{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, sma4))`, against `{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, sma3))`
for three periods.

::: {.charcoal}
**All else equal, choose the forecast with the lower MAD.** Increasing $p$
always smooths *more* — the forecast moves less from period to period and
responds less to the latest data. Whether that lowers the error depends
entirely on the series. Here it helps a lot, and it is worth asking why: a
four-quarter average contains one of every season, so the seasonal spikes
cancel inside the average. A three-quarter average never does. That is not a
coincidence you should count on for a different series.
:::

```{python}
#| label: sma-curve
tune_sma(CAR_SALES, max_p=6).round(2).T
```

The row for $p = 1$ is the naive forecast. Read across: the MAD does not fall
smoothly as $p$ grows. It jumps around, and the even windows win — which is the
seasonal pattern again. (The $p = 6$ MAD averages only six errors; do not read
too much into it.)

```{python}
#| label: sma-plot
_ = forecast_plot(CAR_SALES, {"SMA p=3": sma3, "SMA p=4": sma4},
                  title="Brandywine Ford: actual vs. moving-average forecasts",
                  ylab="Cars sold")
```

The dashed lines are smoother than the actual series: that is the point of
the method, and also its weakness. Every peak is forecast late and low; every
trough is forecast late and high. A moving average *lags*.

## The Weighted Moving Average

::: {.blue}
A **weighted moving average** (WMA) applies weights to the $p$ most recent
values, conventionally giving the most recent value the largest weight. The
denominator is the sum of the weights:

$$\text{WMA}(p=3, t) = \frac{3A_{t-1} + 2A_{t-2} + 1A_{t-3}}{3 + 2 + 1}.$$
:::

The reasoning is that last month probably tells you more about next month than
the month before it did. For Brandywine Ford with weights 3, 2, 1:

```{python}
#| label: wma-math
#| output: asis
show_math(r"\text{WMA}(2019\text{Q1}) = \frac{(3)(%d) + (2)(%d) + (1)(%d)}{6} = \frac{%d}{6} = %.1f"
          % (a[-1], a[-2], a[-3], 3*a[-1] + 2*a[-2] + a[-3], (3*a[-1] + 2*a[-2] + a[-3]) / 6))
```

```{python}
#| label: wma-table
wma = wma_forecast(CAR_SALES, [1, 2, 3])     # weights run oldest -> newest
error_table(CAR_SALES, wma).round(1)[["actual", "forecast", "error", "abs_error"]]
```

MAD `{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, wma))`: a little better than the three-period
SMA (`{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, sma3))`), not as good as the four-period SMA
(`{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, sma4))`). The SMA is a WMA with equal weights.
The choice of weights is arbitrary and found by trial and error — which is a
polite way of saying that if you try enough weights you will find some that fit
the past well, and there is no guarantee they fit the future.

## Two More Yardsticks

MAD is the textbook's measure and the one you should be able to compute by
hand. Two companions are worth knowing because the challenge is scored on more
than one series, and they answer slightly different questions.

::: {.blue}
The **root mean squared error** squares the errors before averaging, so one
large miss counts for more than several small ones:
$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\sum (A_t - F_t)^2 / n}$.

The **mean absolute percentage error** divides each error by the actual value,
so it is unit-free: $\text{MAPE} = \frac{100}{n}\sum |A_t - F_t| / |A_t|$.
A MAPE of 2% on the CPI and a MAPE of 4% on jobless claims can be compared; a
MAD of 1.2 index points and a MAD of 8,000 claims cannot.
:::

```{python}
#| label: summary-cars
accuracy(CAR_SALES, {"naive": nv, "SMA p=3": sma3, "SMA p=4": sma4,
                     "WMA 3-2-1": wma}).round(2)
```

The last column matters. Each method is judged on a different number of
errors, because each needs a different number of periods to get started. With
twelve observations that is a real limitation; with twelve *years* of monthly
data it is not.

# The Challenge Series: the CPI

Now a series you will actually forecast. The Consumer Price Index measures the
price of a fixed basket of goods relative to 1982–84 = 100. It is monthly,
seasonally adjusted, and revised rarely.

## Look before you forecast

Chapter 1 taught you to check a data set before analysing it. That does not
stop being true because the next step is a forecast.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-check
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}")
checks = pd.Series({
    "observations": len(cpi_raw),
    "first": str(cpi_raw.index.min().date()),
    "last": str(cpi_raw.index.max().date()),
    "type": str(cpi_raw.dtype),
    "missing": int(cpi_raw.isna().sum()),
    "missing at": ", ".join(str(d.date()) for d in cpi_raw.index[cpi_raw.isna()]) or "—",
})
checks.to_frame("CPIAUCSL")
```

There is a hole. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish a CPI for
October 2025, because the price survey was not conducted during the federal
shutdown. FRED shows a `.`, and a `.` is not a zero. A moving average needs
consecutive months, so we must decide what to do about it, and the decision is
a modelling choice that belongs in your write-up, not a cleaning step that
happens silently. Here we draw a straight line between September and November
and say so.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-fill
cpi = fill_gaps(cpi_raw, "interpolate")
recent = cpi.loc["2022-01-01":]
```

The second decision is the window. The CPI runs back to 1947 on FRED (1970 in
our file). The 1970s are real data, but they are not the regime you are
forecasting. We use January 2022 onward — `{python} str(len(recent))` months.
How far back to look is a choice; a different window gives a different
forecast, and you should know by how much.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-plot
_ = time_series(recent.index, recent.values,
                title="CPI, all urban consumers, since 2022", ylab="Index, 1982–84 = 100")
```

## Forecast next month

```{python}
#| label: cpi-methods
next_month = (recent.index[-1] + pd.offsets.MonthBegin(1)).strftime("%B %Y")
cpi_methods = {
    "naive":     naive_forecast(recent),
    "SMA p=2":   sma_forecast(recent, 2),
    "SMA p=3":   sma_forecast(recent, 3),
    "SMA p=6":   sma_forecast(recent, 6),
    "WMA 1-2-3": wma_forecast(recent, [1, 2, 3]),
}
cpi_summary = accuracy(recent, cpi_methods)
cpi_summary.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: cpi-best
#| include: false
cpi_best = cpi_summary["MAD"].idxmin()
cpi_worst = cpi_summary["MAD"].idxmax()
```

Forecasts for `{python} next_month` in the first column; the methods are then
judged on every month since 2022 that has a forecast. The smallest MAD belongs
to **`{python} cpi_best`**, and the ranking runs almost exactly opposite to the
car-sales ranking: the widest window is the worst.

::: {.charcoal}
Why? The CPI has a trend. It rises in most months, so *every average of past
values sits below the current level*, and the wider the window, the further
below. A six-month average is forecasting where the CPI was three months ago.
Donnelly says it on p. 770: when a series has a trend or a season, smoothing
methods "lag behind the data, resulting in increased forecasting errors." You
have just watched it happen. The naive forecast lags by only one month, which
is why it wins — for now. After Exam 1 we will meet methods that do not lag at
all.
:::

```{python}
#| label: cpi-forecast-plot
_ = forecast_plot(recent, {"naive": cpi_methods["naive"], "SMA p=6": cpi_methods["SMA p=6"]},
                  title="CPI: the six-month average lags a trending series",
                  ylab="Index", last=24)
```

## Backtest: what the challenge will do to you

The table above judges each method on the whole sample at once. The challenge
does something harsher: every period it asks for one forecast, then reveals the
answer. The fair test of a method is therefore to *replay* that — for each of
the last 24 months, fit the method on the data available at the time, forecast
one month ahead, and record the miss.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-backtest
bt = backtest_summary(recent, {
    "naive":     (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=2":   (sma_forecast, {"p": 2}),
    "SMA p=3":   (sma_forecast, {"p": 3}),
    "SMA p=6":   (sma_forecast, {"p": 6}),
    "WMA 1-2-3": (wma_forecast, {"weights": [1, 2, 3]}),
}, last=24)
bt.round(3)
```

Same verdict, and now it is a verdict you can defend: had you submitted the
`{python} bt["MAD"].idxmin()` forecast every month for two years, you would
have missed by `{python} num(bt["MAD"].min(), 2)` index points on average.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-backtest-detail
backtest(recent, naive_forecast, last=6).round(3)
```

# A Second Series: Weekly Initial Claims

Initial claims for unemployment insurance are released every Thursday for the
week ending the previous Saturday. They are noisy, they have no trend to speak
of in normal times, and they are the most frequently graded series in the
challenge.

```{python}
#| label: claims-setup
claims = icsa.loc["2023-01-01":]
next_week = (claims.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(days=7)).date()
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}")
_ = time_series(claims.index, claims.values,
                title="Initial claims, weekly, since 2023", ylab="Claims")
```

```{python}
#| label: claims-methods
claims_methods = {
    "naive":       naive_forecast(claims),
    "SMA p=2":     sma_forecast(claims, 2),
    "SMA p=4":     sma_forecast(claims, 4),
    "SMA p=8":     sma_forecast(claims, 8),
    "WMA 1-2-3-4": wma_forecast(claims, [1, 2, 3, 4]),
}
accuracy(claims, claims_methods).round(1)
```

```{python}
#| label: claims-backtest
btc = backtest_summary(claims, {
    "naive":       (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=2":     (sma_forecast, {"p": 2}),
    "SMA p=4":     (sma_forecast, {"p": 4}),
    "SMA p=8":     (sma_forecast, {"p": 8}),
    "WMA 1-2-3-4": (wma_forecast, {"weights": [1, 2, 3, 4]}),
}, last=26)
btc.round(1)
```

```{python}
#| label: claims-spread
#| include: false
spread = btc["MAD"].max() / btc["MAD"].min() - 1
```

Forecast for the week ending `{python} str(next_week)`. Over the last 26 weeks
the best method is **`{python} btc["MAD"].idxmin()`**, and the worst is only
`{python} f"{spread:.0%}"` behind it. Claims have no trend, so averaging costs
almost nothing — unlike the CPI, where every average paid for its width. Same
tools, different verdict, and the difference is in the *data*, not the method.

::: {.scarlet}
This is why the challenge makes you look every period rather than pick a method
once in September. The MAPE column says a good week is a 3–4% miss on claims
and a 0.3% miss on the CPI. When you report a forecast, report the error you
expect alongside it. A number without its error is not a forecast; it is a
wish.
:::

# Getting the Data

The syllabus says you should not be transcribing numbers by hand, and it means
it. But there is a constraint you need to know about first.

::: {.scarlet}
**Claude's code sandbox has no internet access.** Claude can run Python on
files you upload; it cannot reach FRED, the LVCVA, or GitHub from inside the
code it runs, whatever your account tier. So every route below ends the same
way: *you* download a file with one click, and Claude reads it. A script that
"downloads the data" is for your own laptop, not for Claude — and if Claude
ever hands you a series it did not read from a file you gave it, it made the
series up.
:::

## FRED: the Download button

Open the series page — <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL> — click
**Download**, choose **CSV**. You get a two-column file, `observation_date`
and `CPIAUCSL`, with a `.` wherever a value is missing. Upload it to Claude
alongside `_forecast.py` and the script you are working from. That is the
whole procedure, for all four FRED series, every week.

If you have Python on your own computer, `scripts/fred_download.py` does the
same thing from the command line and writes a provenance file next to the CSV:

```
python fred_download.py CPIAUCSL ICSA HOUST NVSTHPI
```

If you have a free FRED API key, set it once as the environment variable
`FRED_API_KEY` and the script will use the `fredapi` package as a fallback.
**Never paste the key into a script, a notebook, or a chat.**

## Las Vegas visitor volume: the LVCVA workbook

Visitor volume is not on FRED. The LVCVA posts an Excel workbook for each
year on its [research page](https://www.lvcva.com/research/): a
**Year-to-Date Summary** for the current year and a **Year-End Summary** for
each past year. Row 8 of the first sheet is Visitor Volume, one cell per
month, with an `r` beside any month that has been revised.

`scripts/lvcva_tools.py` — the Python version of the R utilities this course
used before Fall 2026 — reads those workbooks and writes `lv_visitors.csv`.
The procedure inside Claude:

1. On the research page, download the Year-to-Date Summary and the Year-End
   Summaries for 2022 through last year (four or five files, a click each).
2. Start a Claude conversation. Upload the workbooks, `lvcva_tools.py`, and
   `COURSE_CONTEXT.md`. All three are in the
   **[data-tools pack](../upload_packs/lab-16-data-tools.zip)**, together
   with a copy of `lv_visitors.csv` as of the day the note was built, in case
   the LVCVA page is down.
3. Paste this:

::: {.prompt}
Prompt — build the visitor-volume series from the LVCVA workbooks

> I have uploaded several LVCVA "Summary of Monthly Tourism Indicators"
> workbooks and the course file `lvcva_tools.py`. Run
>
> `python lvcva_tools.py <the workbook file names>`
>
> and show me its output verbatim. It should report the year and the number of
> published months it found in each workbook, then write `lv_visitors.csv`.
> Show me the last six rows of that file and the first three, and tell me
> the date of the newest month.
>
> If the script errors on a workbook, show me the traceback and stop. Do not
> type the numbers in from the workbook yourself, and do not fill in a month
> that is not there.
:::

The newest month in the file is the one the LVCVA has published; the
challenge asks you for the one after it. Keep the workbooks: when next month's
summary appears, download the new Year-to-Date file, rerun the same command,
and the series grows by one row — and possibly changes in the row before,
because the LVCVA revises.

On your own computer with Python and internet, `python lvcva_tools.py` with
no arguments finds and downloads the workbooks itself. It pauses a few seconds
between files so as not to hammer a public server; leave the pause in.

## What is in the course packs

Each lab pack ships the CSVs the note was built from. They are a snapshot:
correct on the day they were made and one release behind by the time you read
this. Use them to *learn the method*; use a fresh download to *submit a
forecast*. The `data/README.md` in the repository records the retrieval date
of every file.

# Working with Claude

The Rebel Spark initiative gives you Claude with the full tool suite. That
changes what can be expected of you: the clicking is no longer the skill. The
*specification* is the skill — which series, which window, which method, what
to do about the hole in October 2025 — and so is the *verification*. Below are
prompts that work, the reason they work, and the checks you owe before you
believe the answer.

## The lab prompt

::: {.prompt}
Run this with Claude

> Get the MBA 775 course materials from <https://github.com/jcrooker/mba775>.
> I need `scripts/16a_naive_sma_wma.py`, `scripts/_course.py`,
> `scripts/_forecast.py`, `data/cpi.csv` and `data/icsa.csv`. Read
> `COURSE_CONTEXT.md` from the same repository first — it explains how this
> course expects analytical work to be done.
>
> Run the script and show me its actual output, verbatim. Then walk me through
> what each section does and what the results mean. Do not report any number
> you did not compute, and if anything fails, show me the error rather than
> describing what the output would have been.
>
> If you cannot reach GitHub, tell me plainly and I will upload the files
> instead.
:::

## A bad prompt and a good one

Bad: *"Forecast the CPI for next month."* You will get a number. You will not
know what data it came from, what method produced it, or whether Claude
computed it or remembered a headline.

Good — it names every decision this note asked you to make:

::: {.prompt}
Prompt — a forecast you can defend

> I have uploaded `cpi.csv` (FRED CPIAUCSL, monthly) and `_forecast.py` from my
> course. Using the data from January 2022 onward, and interpolating the single
> missing month (October 2025) — say so in the output — produce a forecast for
> the next month by each of: naive, simple moving averages with p = 2, 3 and 6,
> and a weighted moving average with weights 1-2-3 (most recent weighted 3).
>
> For each method report the next-month forecast, the MAD, RMSE and MAPE over
> the sample, and a rolling-origin backtest over the last 24 months using
> `backtest_summary`. Show the code you ran and its output verbatim. Then tell
> me which method has the lowest backtested MAD and why the wide-window moving
> average does worse on this particular series.
>
> Every number must come from executed code. If a function is missing or
> errors, show me the traceback.
:::

## Verify before you submit

Six checks, each under a minute:

| Check | What it catches |
|---|---|
| The last date printed is the month you think it is | A stale file, or a series that has not updated |
| The forecast is for the *next* period, not the last one | The period-3/period-4 mistake, at scale |
| The MAD was averaged over the right number of errors | A method credited with forecasts it never made |
| Recompute one forecast by hand from the last three values | A method that is not the one you asked for |
| The missing month was mentioned, not silently dropped | A moving average that skipped a month without saying |
| The number in the prose matches the number in the output | The single most common failure: confident prose, different number |

::: {.charcoal}
**Show it fail first.** Try the bad prompt once, on purpose, and run the
checklist against what comes back. The failures are predictable: a forecast for
the wrong period, a figure quoted from memory, a moving average with a
different window from the one you named, a missing month filled without
comment. A student who has caught one of these will check for the rest of their
career. A student handed a working answer has learned nothing.
:::

## Have Claude argue with you

::: {.prompt}
Prompt — a second opinion on your choice

> Here is the backtest table my script produced for weekly initial claims
> (paste it). I plan to submit the SMA p = 2 forecast. Give me the strongest
> case *against* that choice using only the numbers in the table, then tell me
> what I would need to see over the next four weeks to change my mind. Do not
> compute new numbers; argue from these.
:::

## Excel, if you want it

::: {.prompt}
Prompt — a forecasting workbook

> Build an Excel workbook from `cpi.csv`. Sheet `Data`: the raw file, headers in
> row 1. Sheet `Forecast`: columns for date, actual, naive forecast, 3-month
> SMA, 3-2-1 WMA, and the absolute error of each, using live formulas that
> reference the `Data` sheet — no pasted values. The first SMA row must be the
> fourth month, not the third. Put the MAD of each method in a labelled cell at
> the top, computed with `AVERAGE` over the error column, and a line chart of
> actual versus each forecast. Tell me which cells hold formulas and which hold
> constants.
:::

When it opens, change one CPI value and watch which forecasts and MADs move.
The ones that do not are pasted values, and the workbook is wrong.

# Your Turn (from the textbook)

A student wants to forecast her GPA for the fall of her senior year from nine
semesters on a trimester schedule (Donnelly, Your Turn 1 and 2, p. 769–770):

```{python}
#| label: gpa
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}")
gpa = pd.Series([2.5, 2.2, 2.7, 3.0, 2.6, 3.0, 3.2, 2.7, 3.3],
                index=["Fr Fall", "Fr Spring", "Fr Summer", "So Fall", "So Spring",
                       "So Summer", "Jr Fall", "Jr Spring", "Jr Summer"], name="GPA")
gpa.to_frame().T
```

(a) Calculate a two-period SMA forecast for the fall semester of her senior
year and its MAD. (b) Do the same with a two-period WMA with weights 2 and 1.
(c) Which is the better forecast? Do it by hand first; then run the code by
unfolding the block below and check yourself.

```{python}
#| label: gpa-answer
#| code-fold: true
g2 = sma_forecast(gpa, 2)
gw = wma_forecast(gpa, [1, 2])
accuracy(gpa, {"SMA p=2": g2, "WMA 2-1": gw}).round(3)
```

## Your first submission

Once the script runs, you have everything you need for this week's challenge
entries: a forecast, a method, a window, and a measured error. Submit the
forecast in Canvas and keep the script. When the number is published, rerun it
— the new observation goes on the end of the series, the backtest gets one
row longer, and you find out whether your method is still the one you would
choose.

::: {.scarlet}
**What to write down with every submission** (a sentence each): the series and
its last observation date; the method and its parameters; the window of data;
the backtested MAD; and the one thing you would want to know before trusting
the forecast. That is the whole discipline of forecasting, and it fits on an
index card.
:::
